issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Marcel, a 55‑year‑old fashion designer who has spent the last decade designing avant‑garde streetwear in Los Angeles, carries a quiet, palpable tension that colors every aspect of his life. When he was eight, his mother—who had been emotionally unstable—would lift his small frame and slam his head against the kitchen wall, shouting that he was “too loud” and “worth nothing.” The violence was not rare; it came daily, in bursts that left Marcel hollow and trembling, his small body shuddering with each impact. Even in the safety of his own home now, the echo of those blows lingers; he senses a danger in a stranger’s touch, in a sudden silence, and feels as if the world might collapse whenever a wall is closed or a phone rings. He tells his therapist that he sometimes wakes in the middle of the night, eyes wide, heart hammering, the dream images too vivid to name and too frightening to linger. The weight of that early violence has settled into Marcel’s self‑conception. He believes, with a grim certainty, that he has been permanently damaged and that he will never escape the suspicion that others harbor hidden malice. Those negative appraisals seep into his thoughts as he begins each day. He blames colleagues who ask him to finish a garment in a day he cannot meet, and he finds himself dwelling on the wrongs he has done—missing deadlines, refusing to speak up in meetings—while simultaneously accusing others of being untrustworthy. His rumination, both other‑blame and self‑blame, becomes a habitual way of coping; it keeps his mind occupied, preventing the intrusive dreams that haunt him from entering his conscious awareness. The more he believes he is irrevocably harmed, the more he feels the need to keep himself mentally and physically guarded, and the more he steers clear of any situation that might awaken his nightmares. When Marcel’s mind drifts toward memories of that childhood, the images are fragmented, devoid of a clear narrative. He can recall the bruise on his cheek, the cold breath of his mother, the sharp sting of a hammer—yet these details feel detached, almost foreign, as if they belong to someone else’s story. Each recollection is laced with a sudden surge of terror, a startle response that brings the same alarms he experiences during a quiet hallway. The memory of being hit becomes a catalyst for threat; the threat of another blow, of an invisible hand that could still strike, loops back into his mind and forces him to rehearse the past again. In turn, this reheating of images feeds the negative appraisal that he is doomed to repeat the violence or that he might go mad if he cannot control the sensations. The cycle tightens as the more he ruminates—both on his perceived failures and on others’ betrayals—the more fragmented and emotionally numb his recollections become. His avoidance of dreams is a conscious, maladaptive effort to block these memories, but it only makes the fragmented recollections more frequent, as his mind is left to assemble the broken pieces on its own. The constant threat that hovers over him—whether a stranger’s touch, an unexpected silence, or the hush of his own apartment—fuels his sense of being on edge, even when he is alone. This heightened sense of danger exacerbates his belief that he is going insane; he thinks that such hypervigilance is evidence of a mind unraveling. The feeling of mental instability, in turn, reinforces his negative appraisals, cementing the idea that he has become a dangerous, unstable person. As these thoughts spiral, the more he blames himself, the more he avoids even discussing his feelings with anyone, and the more he feels isolated in a world that appears hostile and untrustworthy. The loop is self‑reinforcing: negative appraisals give rise to maladaptive strategies, which in turn amplify memory fragmentation and threat perception, which feed back into the appraisals. Marcel has reached a point where the weight of his internal world feels like a physical burden on his shoulders. He can no longer ignore the mornings he wakes with his heart racing, his palms clammy, convinced that his house is being watched. He has begun to skip meetings with clients out of fear that their questions will trigger a flashback, and he has stopped showing his latest collection to colleagues because the idea of judgment feels like a potential assault. The isolation has cost him a friendship that had begun to bloom, and he has stopped painting in the studio for fear that the rhythm of a brush could trigger a memory. He recognizes that these behaviors are preventing him from living the life he once imagined, yet he cannot bring himself to confront them alone. It is the accumulation of sleepless nights, the growing sense of unreality, and the loss of meaningful connection that finally led him to seek help, hoping to break the tightening cycle and to regain a sense of safety in his own skin. He fears that he will never feel the ease of a quiet home again, but he also longs to reclaim the creative spark that once defined him.
